messages.author: 453ddfeccaf29bbb
messages.subject: i have done the advi pystan thing
parts:
hi allen + everyone else,

GOOD NEWS.

i have written the "missing piece" that, i believe, was stopping us from getting advi into pystan. (thanks ben and jiqiang for your help!)

what's next? i see that you treat the result from optimization and sampling differently. can we write some helper functions for advi too? (it would basically look like a simplified version of what we do for sampling.)

how should we proceed? i don't want to start hijacking the pystan repo at will.

cheers,
alp

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] i have done the advi pystan thing
parts:
> On Apr 24, 2016, at 1:31 PM, Allen B. Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
>
> Without PRs, how do you code review for outside developers who don't
> have the ability to create branches on the repository?

I don't know of any way to do this.

What did you want to accomplish with the pull request?
Why is the pull request being submitted as a work in progress?
To get feedback on design? Feedback on coding? Because there's
some test breaking you can't figure out how to fix?

Is there a way to break it down into smaller pull requests
that are ready to go? Or a way to discuss what the API is
going to be before you start working on it?

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] i have done the advi pystan thing
parts:
Whatever happens, you (Allen) are in charge of the PyStan repo,
so you should use your own judgment and use GitHub however
you see fit.

My own preference is

* email for starting a discussion,

* Wiki for a design/API doc,

* a branch for the code, which you can use to get feedback
on the coding, and

* a pull request when it's ready to be merged and just
needs a final code review.

It's a very ad hoc process, but GitHub's not really set
up to do all of those things well. Lots of people manage this
process separately in other software.

I like the Wiki at the design stage because you can edit it
to be up to date and don't have to try to infer the design
goals from the code.

- Bob
